section.title: Elihu's First Speech
section.sectionRationale: A new voice enters once the three friends fall silent. Elihu, younger and until now quiet out of respect, is angry at Job for justifying himself over God, and angry at the three friends for condemning Job without ever actually refuting him. His opening speech introduces himself as compelled to speak, then turns to Job directly, offering a genuinely new idea: suffering can be God's chastening voice, and there is hope in 'a mediator, one in a thousand,' who can secure a ransom for the sufferer.
section.thesis: Elihu is a distinct voice in the book, neither simply repeating the three friends' failed doctrine of automatic retribution nor fully answering Job's case, but introducing a third possibility: suffering as God's disciplining voice, and a hope in mediation and ransom that reaches toward something Job himself has already longed for.
section.frameNote: Two chapters, eight movements: the narrator's introduction of Elihu's kindled anger; Elihu's explanation for why he must finally speak; his claim to be full of words needing release; his invitation for Job to respond as an equal; his charge that Job is not right in this matter; his teaching that God speaks through dreams and through chastening pain; his striking picture of a mediator who secures a ransom for the sufferer; and his closing call for Job to listen and learn wisdom.

units.label: Elihu's kindled anger
units.note: for justifying himself rather than God

verses.text: So these three men stopped answering Job, because he was righteous in his own eyes.
This {{charah|kindled}} the anger of Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite, of the family of Ram. He burned with anger against Job for justifying himself rather than God,
and he burned with anger against Job’s three friends because they had failed to refute Job, and yet had condemned him.
Now Elihu had waited to speak to Job because the others were older than he.
But when he saw that the three men had no further reply, his anger was kindled.

units.label: Why Elihu must speak
units.note: there is a spirit in a man

verses.text: So Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite declared: “I am young in years, while you are old; that is why I was timid and afraid to tell you what I know.
I thought that age should speak, and many years should teach wisdom.
But there is a spirit in a man, the breath of the Almighty, that gives him understanding.
It is not only the old who are wise, or the elderly who understand justice.
Therefore I say, ‘Listen to me; I too will declare what I know.’
Indeed, I waited while you spoke; I listened to your reasoning; as you searched for words,
I paid you full attention. But no one proved Job wrong; not one of you rebutted his arguments.
So do not claim, ‘We have found wisdom; let God, not man, refute him.’
But Job has not directed his words against me, and I will not answer him with your arguments.

units.label: Full of words
units.note: like a new wineskin about to burst

verses.text: Job’s friends are dismayed, with no more to say; words have escaped them.
Must I wait, now that they are silent, now that they stand and no longer reply?
I too will answer; yes, I will declare what I know.
For I am full of words, and my spirit within me compels me.
Behold, my belly is like unvented wine; it is about to burst like a new wineskin.
I must speak and find relief; I must open my lips and respond.
I will be partial to no one, nor will I flatter any man.
For I do not know how to flatter, or my Maker would remove me in an instant.

units.label: Elihu invites Job to respond
units.note: I too was formed from clay

verses.text: “But now, O Job, hear my speech, and listen to all my words.
Behold, I will open my mouth; my address is on the tip of my tongue.
My words are from an upright heart, and my lips speak sincerely what I know.
The {{ruach|Spirit}} of God has made me, and the breath of the Almighty gives me life.
Refute me if you can; prepare your case and confront me.
I am just like you before God; I was also formed from clay.
Surely no fear of me should terrify you; nor will my hand be heavy upon you.

units.label: You are not right in this matter
units.note: God speaks in one way and in another

verses.text: Surely you have spoken in my hearing, and I have heard these very words:
‘I am pure, without transgression; I am clean, with no iniquity in me.
Yet God finds occasions against me; He counts me as His enemy.
He puts my feet in the stocks; He watches over all my paths.’
Behold, you are not right in this matter. I will answer you, for God is greater than man.
Why do you complain to Him that He answers nothing a man asks?

units.label: God speaks through dreams and pain
units.note: to preserve his soul from the Pit

verses.text: For God speaks in one way and in another, yet no one notices.
In a dream, in a vision in the night, when deep sleep falls upon men as they slumber on their beds,
He opens their ears and terrifies them with warnings
to turn a man from wrongdoing and keep him from pride,
to preserve his soul from the Pit and his life from perishing by the sword.
A man is also chastened on his bed with pain and constant distress in his bones,
so that he detests his bread, and his soul loathes his favorite food.
His flesh wastes away from sight, and his hidden bones protrude.
He draws near to the Pit, and his life to the messengers of death.
Yet if there is a {{melits|messenger}} on his side, one mediator in a thousand, to tell a man what is right for him,
to be gracious to him and say, ‘Spare him from going down to the Pit; I have found his {{kopher|ransom}},’
then his flesh is refreshed like a child’s; he returns to the days of his youth.
He prays to God and finds favor; he sees God’s face and shouts for joy, and God restores His righteousness to that man.
Then he sings before men with these words: ‘I have sinned and perverted what was right; yet I did not get what I deserved.
He redeemed my soul from going down to the Pit, and I will live to see the light.’
Behold, all these things God does to a man, two or even three times,
to bring back his soul from the Pit, that he may be enlightened with the light of life.

units.label: Listen to me and be silent
units.note: for I would like to vindicate you

verses.text: Pay attention, Job, and listen to me; be silent, and I will speak.
But if you have something to say, answer me; speak up, for I would like to vindicate you.
But if not, then listen to me; be quiet, and I will teach you wisdom.”

charah.gloss: To burn, to be kindled with anger. The word describes Elihu's anger four times in the opening verses, both at Job for justifying himself over God and at the three friends for condemning Job without ever actually answering him.

ruach.gloss: Spirit, breath, wind. Elihu claims the Spirit of God has made him and given him life and understanding, the same word used of the breath of life in Genesis 2:7, grounding his authority to speak not in age but in this shared divine gift.

melits.gloss: An interpreter, spokesman, or mediator, one who represents another's case. Elihu's picture of 'one mediator in a thousand' who speaks on the sufferer's behalf is one of the most striking mediatorial images in the Old Testament, anticipating the New Testament's one Mediator between God and man.

kopher.gloss: A ransom, a price paid to cover or redeem a life, from the same root as kaphar, to atone. Elihu pictures the mediator declaring 'I have found his ransom,' language that resonates deeply with the sacrificial and substitutionary themes fulfilled in Christ's atoning death.

basic.context: After the three friends run out of arguments, a younger man named Elihu, who has been listening in respectful silence, finally speaks, angry both at Job for justifying himself rather than God, and at the friends for condemning Job without ever actually proving him wrong. Elihu introduces himself at length, then turns to Job with a genuinely new idea, that suffering can function as God's warning voice, given through dreams or through chastening pain, meant to turn a person from pride, and that there is hope through a mediator who can find a ransom for the sufferer's life.
basic.hermeneutics: Elihu should not simply be read as a fourth version of the friends' failed theology, nor as fully authoritative just because he speaks last before God. The book presents him as a distinct voice: God never rebukes Elihu by name alongside the three friends in 42:7-9, but Elihu's own speeches also contain overconfidence, and his role seems to be preparing Job to hear God rather than delivering the final word himself.
basic.originalLanguages: Elihu's anger, charah, burns against both Job and the friends. He claims the ruach, Spirit, of God has made him and given him life, grounding his right to speak in something deeper than age. And his picture of a melits, mediator, who finds a kopher, ransom, for the sufferer reaches toward hope that goes further than anything the three friends offered.
basic.typology: Elihu's 'mediator, one in a thousand,' who finds a ransom to spare a soul from the Pit, is one of the Old Testament's most vivid anticipations of Christ, our one Mediator, who found not merely a ransom but became the ransom Himself.
basic.christ: Elihu's picture of a mediator who intercedes for the sufferer and secures a ransom price so he is spared from the Pit points directly forward to Jesus Christ, described in 1 Timothy 2:5 as 'the one Mediator between God and men,' who gave Himself as a ransom for all, and in Mark 10:45, who came to give His life as a ransom for many.
basic.god: Elihu insists God is greater than man and speaks in more ways than Job has noticed, through dreams, through pain, and through a mediating voice; this is true as far as it goes, though Elihu, like the friends before him, still assumes he can fully explain God's purposes in Job's specific suffering, a confidence God will gently correct in His own speech.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Timothy 2:5-6 names Christ as the one Mediator who gave Himself as a ransom for all. Mark 10:45 has Jesus describe His own mission in ransom language. Hebrews 12:5-11 develops the theme of suffering as fatherly discipline that Elihu introduces here. Job 42:7-9 notably does not include Elihu among the friends God rebukes.
basic.oneStory: Elihu introduces a genuinely new idea into Job's story: a mediator who can secure a ransom and spare a soul from the Pit. The whole Bible moves toward the fulfillment of exactly this hope in Jesus Christ, the one Mediator between God and humanity, who does not merely announce a ransom has been found but becomes the ransom Himself.

context.literary:
Elihu arrives through the only extended stretch of narrator's prose inside the whole dialogue. Job 32:1-5 stops the poetry to tell us three things: the friends fell silent, Elihu has been waiting, and his anger is burning (the verb of burning turns up four times in these few verses). Nothing like it appears before any other speaker. Then Elihu introduces himself with a full name, Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite, of the family of Ram, a longer introduction than any of the three friends received. His name means, in Hebrew, something like "He is my God," and it is a small ironic frame for a man who is about to speak for God.

The speech has two halves. Job 32:6-22 is a long self-defence addressed partly to the three friends and partly to no one, since in verses 15 to 17 he talks about them in the third person while they stand there. Only Job 33:1 turns to Job by name, and he does so again in Job 33:31 and Job 37:14. Speaking to Job directly, and asking for his reply, is part of what sets Elihu apart.

Chapter 33 then moves in clear steps. Verses 1 to 7 are an assurance that he speaks as a fellow creature, not a judge. Verses 8 to 11 quote Job back to himself. Verses 12 to 30 are the argument: God speaks in dreams (verses 15 to 18), in pain (verses 19 to 22), and through a mediator who brings rescue (verses 23 to 28), all summed up in verses 29 and 30. Verses 31 to 33 close by asking Job to speak or be quiet. The chapter is built around the word Pit, which appears in verses 18, 22, 24, 28 and 30, so the whole speech circles the same question: how does a person come back from the edge of death?

Job does not answer. The silence after 33:33 is one of the strongest features of the speech.
context.historical:
Elihu's polite waiting fits how the book's other speakers think. Bildad tells Job to ask the former generation, Job 8:8-10, and Eliphaz says the gray-haired and aged are on their side, "men much older than your father," Job 15:10. Wisdom belonged to years, and Leviticus 19:32 commands respect for the gray head. Elihu has to argue his way past that expectation, which is why he rests his right to speak on the breath of God, not on age, Job 32:8-9.

His home is Buz. In Genesis 22:21 Buz is the brother of Uz, sons of Nahor, Abraham's brother, so the man belongs to the same wider family as Job, who lived in the land of Uz, Job 1:1. Jeremiah 25:23 still knows Buz among the peoples of the desert edge. The setting is patriarchal: wealth is counted in animals, and the head of the household offers sacrifice for his children, Job 1:3-5. Elihu belongs in that world, and he is described as an outsider to the friends' circle.

Dreams and visions were a normal channel of divine speech in this world. Abimelech is warned in a dream in Genesis 20:3, and Numbers 12:6 lists dream and vision as the ways the LORD speaks to a prophet. Eliphaz has already told of a terrifying vision of the night, Job 4:13-16, and Job himself complains that God frightens him with dreams and terrifies him with visions, Job 7:14. When Elihu says God "opens their ears and terrifies them with warnings," Job 33:16, he is taking up Job's complaint and giving it another meaning.

The Pit and the ransom were also familiar. The Pit is the grave or the realm of the dead, and the ransom, from the law of Exodus 30:12, was a price paid for a life that stood forfeit.
context.canonical:
Elihu's speech is a hinge in the book. Behind it sits Job's cry that there is no mediator between himself and God, "to lay his hand upon us both," Job 9:33, and his hope of a witness in heaven and an advocate on high, Job 16:19-21, and a Redeemer who lives, Job 19:25. Elihu is the first speaker in the book to give that longing a shape: a messenger, one mediator in a thousand, who says "I have found his ransom," Job 33:23-24. Whether Elihu means to answer Job or only to sound clever, the reader hears the two passages side by side.

Beyond Job, the ideas in this chapter spread across Scripture. Ransom is a major theme: Exodus 30:12 speaks of a ransom for the life, and Psalm 49:7-9 says that no man can pay it for his brother, since "the redemption of his soul is costly." Then verse 15 of the same psalm adds the hope that God will redeem my life from Sheol. That is exactly the tension Elihu names and does not solve: someone must pay, and no human can.

The rescue from the Pit becomes the language of thanksgiving. Psalm 103:4 says the LORD "redeems your life from the Pit," Isaiah 38:17 has Hezekiah say that love delivered him from the pit of oblivion, and Psalm 107:17-22 is almost a summary of Job 33:19-28, with the afflicted who loathe food and draw near the gates of death, cry out, and are healed and rescued from the Pit.

The New Testament takes up the discipline theme in Hebrews 12:5-11, quoting Proverbs 3:11-12, and the mediator and ransom themes in Mark 10:45, 1 Timothy 2:5-6, Hebrews 9:15 and 1 Peter 1:18-19. Job 42:7-9 closes the frame by naming only the three friends as wrong, and by making Job himself the one who prays for them.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The writer of Job could have let the three friends' failure stand and gone straight to the whirlwind. Instead he inserts a fourth speaker and takes care to show him as new, angry and sincere. Elihu does two jobs for the book. First, he shows that the friends' defeat was not because Job was right about everything: Elihu is angry at Job for "justifying himself rather than God," Job 32:2, and that concern is real. The book does not want readers to leave thinking that Job's protests were beyond correction. Second, Elihu introduces a fuller account of suffering than mere punishment. He says pain can be a voice, a warning meant to save, Job 33:14-18, and that God is not stuck in a mechanical system of reward and penalty.

The writer also wants readers to notice where Elihu goes wrong. He claims to speak for God, and he claims a special insight, then puts words in Job's mouth that Job never quite said (see Job 33:9 against Job 13:24 and 13:27). He does not know what the reader knows from Job 1 and 2, so he treats affliction as a message to Job about Job. Readers hold that knowledge and can see how a wise idea can wound when misapplied.

For the first hearers, the speech was a call to humility before the God who speaks in many ways and who provides a ransom. It sets the stage for Job's silence and for the LORD's answer, which will not fit into Elihu's explanation, but will not mock it either.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Job 33 describes what one speaker believes about God's ways. It is not a command, and it is not God's verdict. That matters, because Elihu sounds like he is quoting a formula: dream, pain, mediator, ransom, restoration, testimony. Scripture does confirm that God disciplines those He loves, Proverbs 3:11-12 and Hebrews 12:5-11, but the book of Job as a whole refuses to make that a rule for every case. Job's own pain did not come from any sin of his, Job 1:8 and 2:3, and Jesus rejects the reflex to trace every disaster to the sufferer's fault, John 9:1-3 and Luke 13:1-5.

What does carry forward is more modest and more useful. Believers may ask whether a hard season is God's call to turn from something, and remain ready to listen. Those who visit the suffering may not pronounce on the cause. And a person who has been brought back from the brink is meant to say so aloud, as Elihu's rescued man does in front of others, Job 33:27-28. The pattern of open testimony is commended, while the pattern of diagnosing someone else is not.

debates.question: Is Elihu a helpful voice, a foolish one, or something in between?

views.label: A bold but arrogant blunderer
views.case: He talks about himself for seventeen verses before he says a word to Job, Job 32:6-22, claims to be full of words and about to burst, Job 32:18-19, and describes himself as one perfect in knowledge, Job 36:4. He also puts words in Job's mouth that Job never said in that form. Some readers see a young man with more energy than wisdom.

views.label: A transitional voice who prepares for God
views.case: Unlike the friends, he is never named in the LORD's rebuke, Job 42:7-9, he introduces discipline and mediation, ideas the friends never mentioned, and his closing hymn to the storm leads straight into the LORD's answer. On this view he is the necessary step between argument and revelation.

views.label: A partly right speaker whose limits the book lets us see
views.case: The writer gives Elihu true statements (God is greater than man, Job 33:12; God speaks in many ways, Job 33:14) alongside real overreach. God's silence about him neither approves nor condemns him. The reader is left to weigh his words as one weighs any human speech about God.

debates.bearing: The safest reading keeps both facts in view. Elihu is right about more than the friends were, and the book never endorses him as its spokesman. His claim to speak for God is exactly the kind of claim Job warned about in Job 13:7-8, so his best lines have to be tested against the whole book and not treated as final.

debates.question: Who is the mediator of Job 33:23-24?

views.label: An angel who intercedes
views.case: The Hebrew calls him a messenger, and the idea of a heavenly go-between would fit the world of the book, where sons of God appear before the LORD, Job 1:6. The mediator's job is to tell a man what is right for him and to speak up for him.

views.label: A human teacher or prophet
views.case: The word for mediator is used in Genesis 42:23 of the interpreter who stood between Joseph and his brothers. Some hear a wise human interpreter who explains the meaning of suffering to the sufferer, which is what Elihu is trying to do for Job.

views.label: A shadow of Christ
views.case: Whatever Elihu had in mind, the pattern of one who finds a ransom and brings a man back from the Pit finds its full form in Jesus, the one mediator between God and men who gave Himself as a ransom, 1 Timothy 2:5-6.

debates.bearing: These readings are not rivals at every point. Inside the story Elihu most likely pictures an angelic or human helper. Reading the whole Bible, the ransom he mentions is more than any angel or teacher could supply, since Psalm 49:7-8 says no man can pay it, and the New Testament sees the answer in Christ.

study.originalLanguages:
Elihu's own name and the way he describes his anger use one repeated verb. In Job 32:2, 3 and 5, the narrator says his anger was "kindled" or that he "burned," and the same root of burning appears four times in five verses. The BSB smooths the repetition, but Hebrew readers would have felt a fire building. The same idea returns when Elihu says his belly is like unvented wine that is about to burst a new wineskin, Job 32:19. New wine still fermenting was poured into fresh skins because they could stretch, and Elihu describes himself as a skin at its limit. Jesus uses the same image in a different way in Matthew 9:17.

Two words for breath run through his opening claim. In Job 32:8 there is "a spirit in a man, the breath of the Almighty," and in Job 33:4 the "Spirit of God has made me, and the breath of the Almighty gives me life." Ruach is spirit or wind, and neshamah is the breath that God breathed into Adam's nostrils in Genesis 2:7. Job has used the same pair in Job 27:3 to say his life is still in him, and Job 12:10 says the breath of all mankind is in God's hand. Elihu takes shared ground and turns it into a claim about wisdom: every person has that breath, so every person can be taught by it.

In Job 33:6 he says he was "formed from clay." Clay is chomer, the word Job used when he prayed, "You molded me like clay," Job 10:9. Elihu's point is that he is no heavenly rival, only another creature of clay, so Job has no reason to fear him, Job 33:7. He echoes Job's own wish that God's terror would not frighten him, Job 9:34.

The word "chastened" in Job 33:19 comes from a root meaning to reprove, correct or argue a case. It is the same root as the word in Proverbs 3:12, "the LORD disciplines the one He loves," and the sense that Eliphaz used in Job 5:17, "Blessed indeed is the man whom God corrects." It is also the root of the umpire Job longed for in Job 9:33, where the BSB says "mediator." Job wanted someone to decide between him and God, and Elihu says that God Himself is already reproving Job.

The word for "mediator" in Job 33:23 is different again. It comes from a root that describes speaking on behalf of another or translating, and it is the word for the interpreter in Genesis 42:23. Elihu's mediator is a spokesman who carries a message both ways. What he says is the astonishing line "I have found his ransom." Ransom is kopher, the price that covers a life, as in Exodus 30:12 and Psalm 49:7. The same word appears in Job 36:18, where the BSB translates it "bribe," and there it means the payment someone hopes will buy off judgment. The word can point to a rescue or to a corrupt deal, depending on who pays and why.

Finally, the verb "redeemed" in Job 33:28 is the ordinary Hebrew verb of buying back, used in Psalm 49:15 of God redeeming a life from Sheol. And "the Pit," which appears five times in this chapter, is a word for the grave that Psalm 103:4 and Isaiah 38:17 also use. In Job 33:14 and 33:29 the numbers are the way Elihu speaks: "once, yes twice" in the Hebrew of verse 14, and "two or even three times" in verse 29. This numerical style is familiar from Job 5:19 and Psalm 62:11. It says that God does not give up after one warning.

typology.type: The mediator who finds a ransom, Job 33:23-24
typology.fulfillment: Elihu pictures a messenger who stands on the sufferer's side and announces, "Spare him from going down to the Pit; I have found his ransom." In Christ the picture is fulfilled and exceeded. He is the one mediator between God and men, and He does not merely announce a ransom but gives Himself as one, 1 Timothy 2:5-6 and Mark 10:45. Hebrews calls Him mediator of a new covenant who died to redeem, Hebrews 9:15. The type falls short in two ways. Elihu's mediator is one in a thousand, a rare helper, while Christ is the only one. And Elihu's ransom is not identified, whereas the price in the New Testament is the precious blood of Christ, 1 Peter 1:18-19.

typology.type: The rescued man who sings before others, Job 33:26-28
typology.fulfillment: The man who is brought back from the Pit prays, sees God's face and shouts for joy, and then declares in public, "He redeemed my soul from going down to the Pit, and I will live to see the light." This is the shape of resurrection life. Christ, in whom "the light of life" is promised to the Servant after the anguish of His soul, Isaiah 53:11, and who Himself said, "I am the light of the world," John 8:12, is the source. The type is partial because Elihu's man is restored to earthly health, while those united to Christ are raised to life that does not end, Romans 6:9-11. The public song has its answer in the church's thanksgiving, Hebrews 2:12.

Elihu says a man is chastened on his bed with pain, so that his life draws near to the messengers of death. The Old Testament does record discipline of God's people in this way, and Hebrews 12:5-11 draws on Proverbs 3:11-12 to say that God treats believers as sons. The pattern reaches its height in the Son Himself, who "learned obedience from what He suffered," Hebrews 5:8. It differs at once because Christ's suffering was not discipline for any fault, 1 Peter 2:22, and because His pain did what no chastening of ours can do, which is to take our sin away.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ by pattern, at its centre in Job 33:23-24. A sufferer is close to death, no strength of his own can help, and a messenger appears who says, "I have found his ransom." Look at what is being said. The rescue is not the sufferer's repentance, though repentance follows. It is a price found and paid on his behalf, and the result is a body renewed and a face that sees God. The New Testament tells this same story about Jesus with one enormous difference: the mediator is also the ransom. Paul says there is one mediator between God and men, "the man Christ Jesus, who gave Himself as a ransom for all," 1 Timothy 2:5-6. Jesus says He came "to give His life as a ransom for many," Mark 10:45. Peter reminds his readers that they were not redeemed with silver or gold but with the precious blood of Christ, 1 Peter 1:18-19.

It leads to Christ by longing. Job had said there was no mediator between himself and God who could lay a hand on them both, Job 9:33. To do that, a mediator would have to be near enough to a man to touch him and near enough to God to touch Him. Elihu's messenger is one in a thousand and still sits on one side. Only in Jesus, fully man and fully God, is the hand laid on both. Hebrews 12:24 places believers before Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant, and the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word.

It leads to Christ by contrast in Job 33:6, where Elihu says he is just like Job before God, formed from clay, and therefore no threat. The gospel goes further. The Son of God took our clay, sharing in flesh and blood, Hebrews 2:14, so that the mediator would be someone Job could truly approach without terror, the fear Job named in Job 9:34.

It also leads to Christ by the vindication Elihu offers. In Job 33:32 he says, "speak up, for I would like to vindicate you." The desire to declare a person right is a good one. In Christ that desire is carried out, since God justifies the ungodly by the redemption that is in Him, Romans 3:24-26.

There is a caution. Elihu did not know Christ, and his speech does not turn every detail into a code. The dreams, the bed of pain and the number two or three are not pictures of the cross. The link rests on the mediator and the ransom, which the New Testament's own words about Jesus make plain, and on the Servant who bears iniquities so that many may be counted righteous, Isaiah 53:11.
study.god:
The God of this speech is greater than any human accuser. "God is greater than man," Job 33:12, is the sentence on which Elihu hangs his whole argument. It is not meant to shut Job up but to lift the question from a courtroom into a relationship. Job had wanted a trial, with God as the defendant. Elihu insists the two cannot stand on level ground, and the LORD will say something similar from the whirlwind, Job 40:8.

God is a God who speaks. Job had complained that God does not answer, and Elihu replies that He speaks "in one way and in another, yet no one notices," Job 33:14. The complaint is not that God is silent but that His voice comes in forms we may overlook: a warning in the night, a body that will not recover, a friend who tells us the truth. That is a hopeful doctrine, since it means silence is not the same as absence. It is also a demanding one, since it puts the burden of listening on us.

God is a God who rescues from death. Four of the five mentions of the Pit are joined to rescue: preserve the soul, spare him, redeem my soul, bring back his soul. The picture is not a God who delights in pain but one who uses even the edge of the grave to turn a person toward life. "To bring back his soul from the Pit, that he may be enlightened with the light of life," Job 33:30. The same God stands behind Psalm 103:4 and Isaiah 38:17.

God is gracious. In Job 33:24 the mediator is told to be gracious to the man and to say, "Spare him." Grace in the Bible is favour that is not earned. Elihu's man says, "I have sinned and perverted what was right; yet I did not get what I deserved," Job 33:27. That is a confession that God has given him less than his due, and it is the same posture as David's in Psalm 32:5 and Psalm 103:10.

There is a tension the speech cannot resolve, and Scripture does not hide it. God is both the one who chastens and the one who rescues, and Elihu assumes he can tell which is happening in Job. He cannot. The LORD's own answer will not explain Job's pain to him, and it does not follow Elihu's map. For worship, this means we can rejoice that God speaks and saves without claiming to know how He is using any one person's affliction.

crossReferences.note: Job's own longing for a mediator: God is not a man that he can answer, and there is no one to lay a hand on both of them. Elihu's messenger in Job 33:23 reads like an answer, though he stands on one side only. The two passages should be read together because they show how a hope moves from cry to promise.

Job says God frightens him with dreams and terrifies him with visions. In Job 33:15-16 Elihu uses almost the same words, but says the terror is a warning meant to preserve a man from the Pit. The same experience is heard as accusation by Job and as mercy by Elihu.

These are the words Elihu quotes in Job 33:10-11: God counts Job as an enemy, puts his feet in the stocks and watches all his paths. Elihu quotes this part accurately. What he adds, that Job said he was pure and without transgression, goes further than Job did, since Job also spoke of the sins of his youth in Job 13:26.

No man can redeem his brother or pay his ransom to God. The psalm names the impossibility that Elihu's mediator overcomes. Psalm 49:15 then states the hope that God Himself will redeem the psalmist from Sheol, which is the direction the whole Bible moves.

Fools afflicted for their rebellion loathe all food and draw near the gates of death, cry out, and are healed and rescued from the Pit. This is Job 33:19-28 in the form of a thanksgiving song. It shows that Elihu's pattern is a real biblical one, and that the right response is public praise.

Quoted in Hebrews 12:5-6. The LORD disciplines the one He loves, as a father the son in whom he delights. This is the principle behind Job 33:14-22, and it supplies the loving motive that makes pain bearable without making it always the result of sin.

Develops what Elihu only sketches. Discipline is the mark of sonship, it is painful at the time, and later it yields a harvest of righteousness and peace. It applies to believers as a general truth, and it does not let anyone read a particular illness as a particular sin.

There is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave Himself as a ransom for all. Elihu's one in a thousand becomes the one and only, and the ransom he says he has found is the mediator himself.

Jesus says the Son of Man came to give His life as a ransom for many. The word is not a metaphor for moral example. It names a price paid to buy people back, the very thing Job 33:24 promises and Psalm 49:7-8 says no human can supply.

When the LORD finally speaks to the friends, Elihu is not among those rebuked, and Job becomes the one who prays for them. The verdict leaves Elihu's status open, and it shows Job as an intercessor, a small foretaste of the mediator Elihu described.

Hezekiah, brought back from the edge of death, says that love delivered him from the pit and that his sins were cast behind God's back. It matches the rescued man in Job 33:28, and it shows that deliverance from the Pit and forgiveness of sin were bound together in Israel's experience.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with life given by the breath of God, Genesis 2:7, and Elihu opens his speech by resting on that fact: the Spirit of God made him, and the breath of the Almighty gives him life, Job 33:4. Everything that follows in the chapter depends on where that breath goes. After the fall the story becomes a race toward the Pit, and the refrain of Genesis 5 is "and then he died." Elihu's speech is one of the most concentrated pictures in the Old Testament of a person on that road, with flesh wasting, bones showing, and life drawing near to the messengers of death, Job 33:21-22.

What it sets up is the question the rest of Scripture spends itself answering: who can pay? Job 33:24 names the ransom without naming the price. Psalm 49 says no human can afford it. The Passover lamb, the redemption of the firstborn and the atonement money of Exodus 30 all rehearse the principle that a life is bought with a life. The prophets sharpen the longing. Isaiah 43:3 has God give nations as a ransom, and Isaiah 53 has one Servant bear the iniquities of many and see the light of life afterwards.

Job is also part of the movement toward that answer. His cry for a mediator, Elihu's messenger, and Job's own prayer for his friends in Job 42:8-9 are three notes of one chord. None of them is the cure, but each is a place the story is looking toward.

The New Testament resolves the theme. Jesus does not send a messenger with a report that a ransom has been found. He comes as the messenger and pays it, Mark 10:45. He is raised, and the rescued life He gives is not a return to youth but a share in His own resurrection life, Romans 6:9-11. The believer's public testimony, "He redeemed my soul from going down to the Pit," becomes the church's song.

The new creation is where the Pit loses its claim. There will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain, Revelation 21:4, and God's servants "will see His face," Revelation 22:4. Elihu's rescued man sees God's face and shouts for joy, Job 33:26. In the end every redeemed person does the same.

sermon.title: Job: Rebuked in Suffering
sermon.why: Piper's sermon on Job 32:1-37:24 addresses Elihu's introduction and first speech directly, presenting Elihu's view that Job's suffering, though not punishment, served to purge pride from his life, a reading that engages precisely the mediator and discipline themes of Job 33.

quiz.q: Why is Elihu angry, according to 32:2-3?

options.text: At Job for justifying himself rather than God, and at the three friends for condemning Job without ever refuting his arguments.
options.note: Both angers are stated explicitly and directed at different failures in the preceding debate.

options.text: Only at Job, for no stated reason.
options.note: Elihu's anger is directed at both Job and the three friends, for distinct reasons.

options.text: Mostly at the three friends, for failing to actually refute Job's arguments despite condemning him.
options.note: Close, this captures Elihu's frustration with the friends well, but he is also explicitly angry at Job himself, 32:2, not only at the friends.

options.text: At God, for allowing Job's suffering.
options.note: Elihu's anger is directed at the human speakers in the debate, not at God.

quiz.q: On what basis does Elihu claim the right to speak, despite being younger than the others?

options.text: The Spirit of God gives understanding regardless of age; wisdom is not only for the old.
options.note: Verses 8-9 make this argument explicitly, grounding his authority in the Spirit rather than years lived.

options.text: He claims to be older than he actually is.
options.note: Elihu openly states he is young, 32:6, and does not misrepresent his age.

options.text: He claims special revelation that overrides all Scripture.
options.note: He appeals to the Spirit's common gift of understanding, not a claim to override revealed truth.

options.text: He claims that long life experience is usually, though not always, necessary for wisdom.
options.note: Close to his actual nuance in verse 9, but it understates his stronger claim that the Spirit, not age, is the real basis of understanding.

quiz.q: What new idea does Elihu introduce about suffering in 33:19-30?

options.text: Suffering can function as God's chastening voice, turning a person from pride, with hope offered through a mediator who secures a ransom.
options.note: This is a genuinely new angle, distinct from the friends' simple 'suffering equals punishment for specific sin.'

options.text: Suffering is always direct punishment for a specific named sin.
options.note: This was the three friends' position; Elihu's view of discipline and mediation is more nuanced.

options.text: Suffering is primarily meant to punish specific, identifiable sins.
options.note: Close to the three friends' older view, but Elihu's genuinely new idea is that suffering can also work preventatively, turning a person from pride before it fully takes hold.

options.text: Suffering proves God does not exist.
options.note: Elihu's entire argument assumes and affirms God's active involvement in human suffering.

quiz.q: How does Elihu's picture of a 'mediator, one in a thousand' who finds a 'ransom,' 33:23-24, connect to the New Testament?

options.text: It anticipates Christ, described as the one Mediator between God and men who gave Himself as a ransom for all.
options.note: 1 Timothy 2:5-6 and Mark 10:45 use strikingly similar mediator and ransom language fulfilled in Jesus.

options.text: It mainly reflects an ancient Near Eastern idea about angelic intercessors, with only indirect relevance to the New Testament.
options.note: Partly true about the ancient background, but the language of mediator and ransom maps so closely onto 1 Timothy 2:5-6 that most readers see it as a genuine, not merely indirect, anticipation of Christ.

options.text: It proves salvation is achieved by human effort alone.
options.note: The passage emphasizes a mediator acting on the sufferer's behalf, not the sufferer's own effort.

options.text: It teaches that angels, not Christ, are humanity's only hope.
options.note: While Elihu may originally picture an angelic intercessor, the New Testament reveals the pattern's fullest meaning in the one Mediator, Christ.

quiz.q: What is notable about how God treats Elihu in the book's epilogue, 42:7-9?

options.text: God rebukes Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar by name, but does not include Elihu among those corrected.
options.note: This omission is the strongest textual clue that Elihu occupies a different, more preparatory role than the three friends.

options.text: God specifically praises Elihu above all the other speakers, including Job.
options.note: God does not single out Elihu for praise either; he is simply absent from the list of those rebuked.

options.text: God says nothing explicit about Elihu at all, leaving his exact standing unresolved by silence.
options.note: Very close to correct, though it does not name the specific and significant detail that Elihu is absent precisely from the rebuke given to the three friends by name.

options.text: Elihu is included among the three friends who must be forgiven by Job.
options.note: Only Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar are named as needing Job's intercessory prayer, 42:8-9.

questions: Elihu waited respectfully before speaking, then felt compelled once he had something true to say. How do you discern the right time to speak up versus the wisdom of staying quiet a while longer?

Elihu suggests that pain can be God's way of turning someone from pride they cannot otherwise see in themselves. Is there a hard season you can now see, in hindsight, refined something in you that comfort never would have touched?
Elihu's picture of a mediator who finds a ransom for a dying soul points forward to Christ. How does knowing Jesus is your Mediator change how you approach God when you feel far from Him?

Elihu claims special insight from the Spirit while still being capable of overconfidence in his own judgment. How do you hold conviction about what you have learned from God alongside real humility about what you might still be missing?
Job never responds to Elihu directly in the text. Have you ever received counsel that was partly right but that you were not yet ready to fully receive? What helped you eventually weigh it fairly?

translationNotes.note: 'My belly is like unvented wine' pictures Elihu's pent up words as fermenting wine pressing against its skin, a vivid image of internal compulsion to speak that the BSB renders literally from the Hebrew idiom.
'Formed from clay' echoes the creation language of Genesis 2:7, and is Elihu's way of leveling the playing field with Job, insisting he speaks as a fellow creature, not a superior judge.

'Messenger' translates melits, which can mean an interpreter, spokesman, or mediator; older English translations sometimes render it 'interpreter,' but 'mediator' better captures its function of representing the sufferer's case and securing a ransom.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched via the makor-scripture toolkit for Job 32:1-33:33.
